analysis.one_liner: Lets families sue private detention centers $5 million and up when someone dies in their custody.
analysis.headline: Introduced in July 2026 with three Democratic cosponsors, the bill was sent to the House Judiciary Committee and has received no hearing, vote, or floor action since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let the family of anyone who dies in a privately operated detention facility — for example, an immigration detention center run by a private company under federal contract — sue that company in federal court. It sets damages of at least $5 million per death, adds economic and punitive damages, holds the company itself responsible for its employees' actions, and bars the company or its workers from using immunity defenses. It was introduced in July 2026 and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, where it has not moved.
analysis.who_benefits: The main beneficiaries are the families of people who die while held in privately run federal detention facilities — including immigration detainees and federal prisoners housed by private contractors. The bill gives them a federal lawsuit with a guaranteed $5 million minimum in damages, plus economic and punitive damages, and strips the company and its employees of immunity defenses that often end such cases. It also creates a deterrent that affects everyone held in private detention, since companies facing certain large payouts have a stronger financial reason to prevent deaths in the first place.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Families of people in private detention

how_it_helps.text: It creates a private right of action, meaning the family of a person who dies in a private detention center can sue in federal court without needing the government to prosecute first.
It sets statutory damages of not less than $5 million plus economic damages, and allows punitive damages on top.
It holds the private detention company itself responsible for deaths caused by its employees, so families are not limited to suing low-level workers.
It blocks company officers and employees from using absolute or qualified immunity — defenses that often defeat lawsuits against people acting under government authority.

analysis.who_pays: Private detention contractors and their shareholders would bear the cost of lawsuits and settlements, and would face pressure to spend more on staffing, medical care, and safety inside their facilities. Some of that cost could flow indirectly to taxpayers if companies raise the prices on their federal detention contracts to cover the new liability.

drawbacks.text: The bill sets a floor of $5 million in statutory damages for every wrongful death, regardless of the circumstances, on top of economic and punitive damages — a flat minimum that applies even where the facility's failure was less severe, which an honest supporter would acknowledge is a blunt instrument.

Because these facilities operate through federal contracts, a large new liability exposure could be reflected in contract pricing, meaning some of the cost could ultimately flow back to federal taxpayers rather than only to the companies' shareholders.

Detained people already can bring some tort and civil rights claims under existing law; the bill adds a new federal route with much larger guaranteed damages, and critics would argue that overlaps with and federalizes claims currently handled under state law.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real: a family whose relative dies in a privately run detention facility would get a federal courtroom and a floor of $5 million in damages, with no immunity escape hatch — a serious deterrent that does not exist today. The strongest good-faith objection is that a fixed multi-million-dollar minimum applies to every death regardless of how much the facility actually failed, which could push liability costs into federal contract prices paid by taxpayers and could pressure private operators out of the market in ways that affect where detainees are held. Those costs are borne by a profitable industry and, indirectly, taxpayers, while the benefit accrues to detained people and their families — a trade most readers would likely accept, though the blunt statutory minimum is a design weakness.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Judiciary Committee, where it has sat with no hearing or vote ever scheduled.

narrative.text: Rep. Derek Tran introduced the bill in the House on July 22, 2026.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary — the only action it has received.
Three House Democrats — Seth Moulton, Bonnie Watson Coleman, and Shri Thanedar — signed on as original cosponsors; no Republican has.
The Judiciary Committee has held no markup and the House has taken no vote on the bill, and with the Congress ending January 3, 2027, it would need to be reintroduced to survive.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private detention companies, which face no new liability as long as the bill stays in committee; families of people who die in private custody remain with the limited remedies available under existing law.

for.name: Rep. Derek Tran
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill creating a private right of action for wrongful deaths in private detention centers.

for.name: Reps. Seth Moulton, Bonnie Watson Coleman, and Shri Thanedar
for.what_they_did: Joined as cosponsors at introduction, the only members supporting the bill on record.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee (Chair Jim Jordan)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on July 22, 2026 and has taken no further action — no hearing or markup on the bill has been scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: All four supporters are Democrats and no Republican has cosponsored; with Republicans controlling the House and its committees, the bill has not moved past referral.

industries.industry: Private prison and immigration detention companies
industries.note: Companies that hold federal detainees under contract (such as GEO Group and CoreCivic) would face lawsuits with a $5 million minimum in statutory damages per death, plus punitive damages, with no immunity defenses and liability attached to the company itself. This is a direct financial threat to their current operating model, in which liability and accountability for deaths largely stays with the government or individual workers.

analysis.trajectory: Bills introduced this late in a two-year Congress with no cosponsors from the majority party rarely reach the floor. With no committee action scheduled and a Republican-controlled House, the most likely outcome is that the bill dies in committee at the end of this Congress unless a supporter reintroduces it in the next one.
